summary: Specifies how to use Datagram Transport Layer Security over DCCP. DTLS gives privacy and tamper detection to datagram applications, and DCCP provides a congestion-controlled but unreliable datagram service. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: This puts a secret lock on messages sent by a transport that checks for congestion but does not guarantee delivery.

questions: how does dtls work with dccp
what is a dccp service code
subtitle: How to carry DTLS-secured traffic inside DCCP packets, and where the two protocols' rules meet.

tldr.problem: Applications that use DCCP's congestion-controlled but unreliable datagram service had no standard way to get the privacy and tamper detection that DTLS gives other transports.
tldr.mechanism: DTLS records are placed whole in the Application Data field of DCCP-Data and DCCP-DataAck packets, and the RFC settles how handshakes, retransmission timers, path MTU and Service Codes interact.
tldr.outcome: DCCP applications get transport security similar to what TCP, UDP and SCTP applications have. RFC 5238 is updated by RFC 8996.

facts.label: Record placement
facts.value: Whole record in a single packet

today: RFC 5238 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8996. It has not been obsoleted. Its approach is written to apply to future versions of DTLS.

sections.title: Why DTLS Over DCCP
sections.content:
This document specifies how to carry application payloads with Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS, RFC 4347) in the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP, RFC 4340).

DTLS is TLS adapted for the unreliable transport UDP, so it is TLS plus adaptations for unreliability. DCCP offers an unreliable service like UDP but with adaptive congestion control like TCP and SCTP; it can be seen as UDP-plus-congestion-control or TCP-minus-reliability, and unlike TCP it offers multiple congestion control algorithms. Together they give DCCP applications transport security similar to that available for TCP, UDP and SCTP.
sections.eli5: One tool locks messages so nobody can read or change them. Another tool sends messages while watching for traffic jams. This RFC shows how to use both together.

sections.title: Putting DTLS Records in DCCP Packets
sections.content:
The approach is straightforward: DTLS records are sent in the Application Data field of DCCP-Data and DCCP-DataAck packets. Several DTLS records MAY share one packet, as long as it stays within the Path Maximum Transfer Unit (PMTU) in force when fragmentation is not allowed, or within the current DCCP maximum packet size when it is. A single DTLS record MUST be fully contained in one DCCP-Data packet and MUST NOT be split across packets.

DCCP and DTLS both use sequence numbers, but they serve only partly overlapping functions. The RFC says there is no connection between the sequence number of a DCCP packet and the one in a DTLS record inside it, and none between related features such as DCCP synchronization and DTLS anti-replay protection.
sections.eli5: Each locked envelope goes whole into one DCCP package. You can put several envelopes in a package, but you may never cut one in half.

sections.title: Handshakes and Connection Lifetimes
sections.content:
Both protocols are connection-oriented and have their own handshakes. Following the mapping above, the DCCP handshake comes first and the DTLS handshake second, as with TLS over TCP. But DCCP-Request and DCCP-Response have Application Data fields, so the handshakes can partly overlap. A DTLS client MAY send one or more DTLS records, typically handshake messages, in the DCCP-Request. A DTLS server MAY process them and reply in the DCCP-Response, or delay its answer until the DCCP handshake completes and send it in a DCCP-Data packet.

That data is not reliable: a DCCP server can discard Application Data in a DCCP-Request, and a retransmitted request or response may leave the original data out. DTLS retransmits lost handshake records, but records first sent in a Request or Response can only be resent after the DCCP handshake completes. Both protocols retransmit after normally 1 second and double the timer, so DTLS over DCCP MUST wait for the DCCP handshake to complete before restarting its DTLS handshake retransmission timer.

A DTLS connection runs entirely inside the life of its DCCP connection. Several DTLS connections can be resumed from one DTLS session, each over its own DCCP connection, and a session can also be resumed over a different transport. Applications MUST NOT send unprotected data on a DCCP connection that is also carrying a DTLS connection, because that allows packet insertion attacks.

Processing a DTLS handshake is relatively CPU intensive. An application that starts DTLS connections in series over one DCCP connection SHOULD limit the burden, for example with a minimum of 1 second between session initiations.
sections.eli5: The two hello rituals can be done at the same time to save a trip, but notes passed during the first ritual might get dropped. So the second ritual waits its turn before trying again.

sections.title: Congestion Control Effects
sections.content:
DTLS handshake messages can be large, so DCCP congestion control may slow them enough that DTLS times out and retransmits, which can make congestion worse. The RFC notes that a DTLS-over-UDP application in the same network would not necessarily do better, since UDP has no slow-start or congestion control. It quotes RFC 4347 that mishandling the retransmission timer can lead to serious congestion problems.

Implementations SHOULD avoid retransmitting a request that DCCP has queued but not yet sent, when DCCP can report this, for example by starting the timer only once the message has passed to the IP layer.

A big handshake can also leave congestion control in a state unsuited to the data that follows. With CCID 2 (RFC 4341), which uses an additive increase multiplicative decrease (AIMD) algorithm like TCP, a large handshake may cause a decrease the application data would not have caused. Applications for which this matters should consider CCID 3 (RFC 4342), which uses TCP-Friendly Rate Control (RFC 3448) and varies the allowed rate more slowly.
sections.eli5: If a huge locked package goes first on a busy road, DCCP may slow everything down. Waiting too impatiently and sending the package again only makes the traffic worse.

sections.title: Path MTU and Record Size
sections.content:
Each DTLS record must fit in a single DCCP-Data packet. DCCP normally sends with the Don't Fragment bit set for IPv4 (or no fragmentation extension headers for IPv6), so it performs PMTU Discovery. DTLS does too, with a very similar algorithm. A DTLS over DCCP implementation MAY use the DCCP-managed PMTU and skip its own discovery, but SHOULD still follow Section 4.1.1.1 of RFC 4347 for fragmenting handshake messages during retransmission. Alternatively it MAY do its own discovery but MUST NOT use a value greater than the one DCCP determined.

When an application resets the PMTU estimate, the implementation SHOULD also reset DCCP's estimate. It SHOULD also control the DF bit or fragmentation headers in DCCP in line with the application's wishes, when DCCP supports that.

The DCCP maximum packet size (MPS) is bounded by the congestion-control-state limit (CCMPS), can vary over time, and may be smaller than the 65,535 bytes normally used in UDP. A DTLS record size MUST NOT exceed the DCCP MPS currently in force.
sections.eli5: Every package must fit through the door of the road, and the door size can change. So the envelope must never be bigger than the door is right now.

sections.title: Service Codes and Future DTLS Versions
sections.content:
The DCCP handshake carries a Service Code describing the application-level service the client wants, which helps middleboxes and reduces reliance on well-known ports. Since many middleboxes are expected to treat DTLS over DCCP differently from plain DCCP, an application that uses both modes SHOULD register and use a different Service Code for each. It MAY listen on the same DCCP port and tell the modes apart by Service Code. An application that starts without DTLS and switches to it on the same connection must use one Service Code, because it cannot be changed after the connection is established.

DTLS records are carried transparently, so this document is assumed to apply to all future versions of DTLS, and will be revised only if a change to DTLS or DCCP (including its CCIDs) requires it. An application moving to a new DTLS version is RECOMMENDED to keep its Service Code and let DTLS handle version negotiation, though it MAY register a new one if the new version significantly changes middlebox-relevant behavior.
sections.eli5: A Service Code is a label on the package saying what it is for. If locked and unlocked packages need different treatment on the way, they should have different labels.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC points to RFC 4347 for DTLS and RFC 4340 for DCCP, and states that combining them introduces no new security considerations. The practical cautions in the body still apply: never mix unprotected data into a DTLS-carrying DCCP connection, and limit how fast new DTLS sessions can be started.
sections.eli5: Mixing the two does not make new dangers, but you must not slip unlocked mail into the locked mailbag, and you should not let someone keep asking you to start new locked chats all day.
